questions.question: You swap the Q-table for a neural net and run plain Q-learning on Atari frames, changing nothing else. What does the lesson say happens?
options: It works, just slowly, since a network generalizes across visually similar frames
It diverges — the combination has no convergence guarantee
It overfits the first episode and the gradients collapse to zero
It converges to Q^π for the exploration policy rather than to Q*
questions.explanation: Function approximation plus bootstrapping plus off-policy learning is the deadly triad, and no theorem covers it. Replay and the target network exist specifically to make the combination behave in practice.

questions.question: What does sampling minibatches uniformly from a replay buffer buy you?
options: A lower-variance estimate of the full discounted return
An unbiased sample from the current policy's state distribution
Decorrelated updates, and repeated use of rare transitions
A guarantee that every state-action pair is visited infinitely often in the limit
questions.explanation: Successive Atari frames are nearly identical, so consecutive on-policy gradient steps would be almost the same step. Shuffling a large buffer breaks that correlation and lets one lucky reward teach the net many times.

questions.question: Why keep a second, frozen copy of the network for the Bellman target?
options: To halve the memory the backward pass needs
So the regression target holds still while θ keeps moving
To supply the exploration noise that ε-greedy needs when Q values are still flat
So the two networks can vote on which action is greedy
questions.explanation: With one network on both sides of the equation you are regressing onto your own shifting output. Freezing θ⁻ turns each interval into an ordinary supervised regression problem.

questions.question: How does Double DQN change the target computation?
options: It takes the minimum over two independently trained target networks
It clips the target into {-1, 0, +1} before the regression
It averages the target produced by the online net and the target net
The online net picks the argmax; the target net evaluates it
questions.explanation: Selection and evaluation then rest on independently noisy estimates, so the noise no longer conspires to inflate the max. It is a drop-in change and consistently better.

questions.question: Your rewards are dollar amounts from 1 to 5000 and DQN training is unstable. Which move does the lesson sanction, and what is the catch?
options: Normalize the reward scale; you may discard information magnitudes carry
Push γ toward 1.0; you also lengthen the credit-assignment horizon considerably
Shrink the replay buffer; you also lose the rare transitions
Sync the target net every step; you also lose the frozen target
questions.explanation: Gradient magnitude scales with reward magnitude, so a 5000× spread dominates every update. Atari-style sign clipping is only correct when the sign is all that matters — for dollars it usually is not.

questions.question: You set the target-network sync interval to every single step. What have you effectively built?
options: Double DQN, since selection and evaluation now use the same weights
DQN with no target network at all
A soft-update (Polyak) variant
An on-policy SARSA agent
questions.explanation: Syncing every step means θ⁻ is always θ, which is precisely the moving-target instability the second network was introduced to remove. The opposite extreme, syncing too rarely, gives you stale targets instead.
